While I agree that there are some concerns here (not as many as clickbait sites would have you believe), statements like this just make me understand this person has absolutely no idea what they are talking about.

As explained in the original article this "niche app" is basically the application of self learning analytic tools in auditing diagnostic and administrative processes. What this basically means is that doctors will have a backup system cross checking and peer reviewing their work in order to prevent human errors from killing people.

It would be able to do things like note that a patient was prescribed a dosage of a given medication is 10 times higher than normally associated with their condition (even if that might be a normal dosage for another condition) and think that someone may have accidentally added a zero. Considering that medical errors are now the third leading cause of death in the US, I don't think the importance of that sould be underestimated.

It would be able to do things like analyze the health history of cancer patients and build models that identify people at high risk so they can be screened more often and catch anything early. I personally would be OK with a third party having anonymous access to my medical records if it meant I don't die because someone has shitty penmanship.

I don't know the rules in NZ, but in the US, an aircraft flying in instrument meteorological conditions has to comply with IFR flight rules. This means that if weather at the destination airport will be below 2000ft ceilings, or less than 3sm visibility, pilots must select a suitable alternate, and carry enough fuel to fly to their destination, the alternate, and then another 45 minutes.

If the weather at the alternate is forecast to be lower than 600ft ceilings, or 2sm visibility, you can't use it as an alternate.

So what probably happened is the weather conditions at both the destination and typical alternate were below minimums, so the airline had to pick a new alternate, and add fuel.
